\chapter{Further Down --- Neck, Shoulder, Back, Knee, Ankle}
\label{ch:mas-del-cuerpo}
\hlchaptermodality{293}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the neck, the shoulder, the back, the knee and the ankle in Spanish, and say which one hurts.}

Complete ES-C293-tobillo: name all five places in order and say that each one hurts.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el cuello]{el cuello — what an accolade was thrown around}

\label{lesson:ES-C293-cuello}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what was \emph{mons}? (A hill.) And what was \emph{lacus}? (Standing water.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cabeza — what sits on top of it.
  \item la garganta — what runs down inside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CUE-llo}, stress on the first part. The \emph{ue} is one slide, and the \emph{ll} is the \emph{y} sound you have had since \emph{cebolla}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el cuello} — \textquotedblleft{}the neck.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{collum}, and there is that \emph{o}-to-\emph{ue} break again, the one you met in \emph{pueblo}. Spanish did it here for exactly the same reason.

\emph{Collum} is all over English clothing and ceremony. A \textbf{collar} is the thing that goes round it. An \textbf{accolade} is \emph{ad collum}, \textquotedblleft{}to the neck\textquotedblright{} — originally the embrace, or the sword laid on the shoulder, that made somebody a knight. The word now means any honour, and has forgotten it used to be a gesture.

\emph{El cuello} does double duty in Spanish, as it does in English: the neck of a person and the neck of a shirt are the same word, and so is the neck of a bottle.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more place on the body, and you already had the ones above it.

\emph{La cabeza}, \emph{la garganta}, and now \emph{el cuello}. Being able to say precisely where something hurts is one of the few pieces of vocabulary that is genuinely urgent, which is why this ground is worth going over twice.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cuello}
  \item \emph{me duele el cuello}
  \item \emph{la cabeza}, \emph{el cuello} — top down
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{collum}? (The neck.) What does \emph{accolade} say, taken apart? (To the neck.) And what break turned \emph{collum} into \emph{cuello}? (Short \emph{o} into \emph{ue}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el hombro]{el hombro — the bone a doctor still names in Latin}

\label{lesson:ES-C293-hombro}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what was \emph{mons}? (A hill.) And what does \emph{accolade} mean, taken apart? (To the neck.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el cuello — what this sits either side of.
  \item la mano — the far end of the same arm.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{OM-bro}, stress on the first part. The \emph{h} is silent — begin on the vowel and the word is right. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el hombro} — \textquotedblleft{}the shoulder.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{umerus}, with no \emph{h} at all. Spanish added the letter later, purely as spelling, and it has been silent from the day it arrived. If you say \emph{ombro} you have said the word correctly.

The Latin survives untouched in English medicine: the \textbf{humerus} is the long bone of the upper arm, running from this joint to the elbow. It is one of those words English kept in a white coat while Spanish wore it every day.

Do not confuse \emph{umerus} with \textbf{humor}, the old bodily fluid — nor with \textbf{humus}, the ground. Three similar Latin words, three unrelated families, and the \emph{h} that Spanish sprinkled on \emph{hombro} makes the confusion easier rather than harder. Spelling is not always your friend.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and they are next to each other on the body.

\emph{El cuello} and \emph{el hombro}. You are working downward, and the run will keep going down — which is a better way to hold a set of body words than any list, because the body supplies the order for you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el hombro}
  \item \emph{me duele el hombro}
  \item \emph{el cuello}, then \emph{el hombro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{umerus}? (The shoulder.) What do doctors call that bone today? (The humerus.) And what is the \emph{h} in \emph{hombro} doing? (Nothing — it is silent.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la espalda]{la espalda — a broad blade, worn on the body}

\label{lesson:ES-C293-espalda}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what was \emph{umerus}? (The shoulder.) And what was \emph{collum}? (The neck.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el hombro — the corner of it.
  \item el dolor — what it is famous for.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{es-PAL-da}, stress in the middle. There is the \emph{e-} step again, in front of \emph{sp}, exactly as in \emph{estrella}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la espalda} — \textquotedblleft{}the back.\textquotedblright{}

Underneath is Latin \textbf{spatula}, a broad flat blade, itself a small \textbf{spatha}, a broad sword. The shoulder blade was named after the tool it resembles, and in Spanish the name spread out from the blade to cover the whole back.

Strip the Spanish \emph{e-} and the English relatives line up. A \textbf{spatula} is still a broad flat blade in a kitchen. A \textbf{spade} is a bigger one. An \textbf{epaulette} is the ornament on a shoulder, through French \emph{épaule} — and French put an \emph{é} on the front for the same reason Spanish put an \emph{e}, so the two languages solved one problem twice.

This is the second word in this run where the \emph{e-} is the only thing standing between you and a word you already know. It is worth making that a habit: meet an unfamiliar \emph{es-} word, take the \emph{e} off, and see what is left.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, still working downward: \emph{el cuello}, \emph{el hombro}, \emph{la espalda}.

The \emph{e-} trick has now paid twice — once on a star and once on a back — which is about the point at which a pattern stops being a curiosity and starts being a tool.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la espalda}
  \item \emph{me duele la espalda}
  \item \emph{el cuello}, \emph{el hombro}, \emph{la espalda}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{spatula} in Latin? (A broad blade.) Which English kitchen tool is the same word? (A spatula.) And what happens if you take the \emph{e-} off an \emph{es-} word? (A familiar word is often underneath.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la rodilla]{la rodilla — a little wheel, which is exactly right}

\label{lesson:ES-C293-rodilla}



\begin{quote}
Quick pass: what was \emph{spatula}? (A broad blade.) What was \emph{umerus}? (The shoulder.) And what was \emph{collum}? (The neck.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la espalda — the word before this one.
  \item el dolor — what this joint tends to produce.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ro-DI-lla}, stress in the middle. The opening \emph{r} is rolled; the \emph{d} between vowels is soft. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la rodilla} — \textquotedblleft{}the knee.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{rota} was a wheel, and \textbf{rotella} a little one. That is what the knee was called: the small wheel in the middle of the leg. Anyone who has watched a kneecap turn will grant that it is a fair description.

\textbf{Rota} is busy in English. To \textbf{rotate} is to wheel. A \textbf{rotary} is a wheel of traffic. \textbf{Roulette} is a little wheel through French — the same diminutive as \emph{rotella}, built in a different language. And something \textbf{rotund} is wheel-shaped.

There is that \emph{-illa} again, and this is the fourth time it has appeared. Once in an onion, once in a seed, and now in a knee. When an ending shows up in words that have nothing to do with one another, it has stopped being decoration and become part of how the language builds things.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, from the neck down to the leg: \emph{el cuello}, \emph{el hombro}, \emph{la espalda}, \emph{la rodilla}.

Each one arrived with a picture attached — a collar, a bone, a blade, a wheel. Words with a picture behind them survive in the memory much longer than words with only a translation.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la rodilla}
  \item \emph{me duele la rodilla}
  \item \emph{el cuello}, \emph{el hombro}, \emph{la espalda}, \emph{la rodilla}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{rota}? (A wheel.) What did \emph{rotella} add? (Smallness.) And which English gambling wheel is the same diminutive? (\emph{Roulette}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el tobillo]{el tobillo — a small lump, honestly named}

\label{lesson:ES-C293-tobillo}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what was \emph{rota}? (A wheel.) What was \emph{spatula}? (A broad blade.) And what was \emph{umerus}? (The shoulder.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la rodilla — the joint above this one.
  \item el dolor — what a twisted one gives you.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{to-BI-llo}, stress in the middle. The \emph{b} between vowels is soft, lips barely touching. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el tobillo} — \textquotedblleft{}the ankle.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it is Latin \textbf{tuber}, a swelling or a lump, with the small ending on it. The ankle is the little lump at the bottom of the leg, and the Romans saw no reason to be more poetic about it than that.

\textbf{Tuber} kept its lumpiness in English. A \textbf{tuber} is the swelling on a root that we eat as a potato. \textbf{Tuberculosis} is named for the small lumps the disease leaves in the lungs. A \textbf{protuberance} is a lump sticking forward, which is \emph{pro-} doing the sticking.

That is the fifth \emph{-illo} or \emph{-illa} in this stretch of the book, and by now it should not need pointing out. A seed, an onion, a knee, an ankle: none of them related, all of them small.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and a whole side of the body: \emph{el cuello}, \emph{el hombro}, \emph{la espalda}, \emph{la rodilla}, \emph{el tobillo}.

Said in that order they run from the top of the spine to the bottom of the leg, and each of them fits straight into \emph{me duele} — which you have had for a long time and which now has five more places to point at. The vocabulary is new; the sentence around it is not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el tobillo}
  \item \emph{me duele el tobillo}
  \item all five — \emph{el cuello}, \emph{el hombro}, \emph{la espalda}, \emph{la rodilla}, \emph{el tobillo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{tuber}? (A swelling, a lump.) Which vegetable part is still called one? (A tuber.) And what do \emph{-illo} and \emph{-illa} add? (Smallness.)
\end{tcolorbox}
